title: Debt or Equity: The Form of the Money Decides What It Costs
summary: When a parent company funds a project company, it can do so as a shareholder or as a lender. The choice changes tax, priority in insolvency, the bank's view and how cash can come back. This lesson teaches the choice as a design decision, made deliberately and documented before the money moves.
body:
Money that enters a project company as a loan and money that enters as shares are the same dollars with different legal lives, and the life you choose decides how they are taxed, who gets paid first and how they come home.

Recall

Q. In foreign-affiliate thinking, why does the line between active and passive income matter?

A. Because many systems tax passive income earned abroad in the hands of the owner as it arises, rather than when it is paid home, to stop income being parked offshore. Active business income is usually left alone until it is distributed. Verify the rules in each country against the primary source.

Q. Name the four main ways cash can leave a project company and reach its owner.

A. Dividend, interest, fee, or return of capital. Each carries different tax treatment and different withholding.

Q. What is a guaranteed maximum price (GMP)?

A. A ceiling on what the owner pays the construction manager or contractor for a defined scope, with costs above it carried by the contractor unless scope changes. It is a contract term, not a standard.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in Week 55 I called structure a design problem. This week we design the plumbing that carries money into the structure. Most small developers fund their project company however is quickest: a wire from the parent, a line in a spreadsheet, and a decision about what to call it made months later by an accountant. By then the choice has already been made by default, and default is rarely the cheapest, the safest or the one a lender will accept. Nadia joins me this week because the choice has to be visible in the books from the first dollar.

Two kinds of money

Plain English first. Equity is ownership. The parent buys shares in the project company. It has no right to be repaid on a date, no right to interest, and it is paid last if the company fails. In return it owns whatever is left after everyone else is paid, which in a good project is most of the upside.

Debt is a promise. The parent lends money to the project company under an agreement that sets an amount, an interest rate, a repayment schedule and what happens on default. The project company owes it whether or not the project makes a profit.

The professional framing is that the parent can hold its investment in a project company through any mix of the two, and that the mix is called the capitalisation of the company. A company funded mostly by loans from its own shareholders, with very little share capital, is described as thinly capitalised. We will meet the rules that push back on that in Day 4.

Why would anyone lend to a company they already own? Four reasons. Interest may be deductible to the project company, reducing tax where the project is. Repayment of principal is usually not taxed as income, whereas a dividend usually is. A loan can rank ahead of ordinary shares if the project fails, so the parent recovers more. And a loan creates a schedule, which disciplines how cash comes back.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example one: the tax effect

Take a hypothetical stabilised project company with net operating income (NOI), the rent left after operating costs, of 1,000,000 dollars a year. Assume, for arithmetic only, a 30 percent tax rate in the project's country. That rate is hypothetical; it is not any real country's rate.

Case A: the parent funds 10,000,000 dollars entirely as shares. Taxable income is 1,000,000 dollars, tax is 300,000 dollars, and 700,000 dollars is left to distribute as a dividend.

Case B: the parent funds 4,000,000 dollars as shares and 6,000,000 dollars as a loan at 6 percent. Interest is 360,000 dollars. If it is deductible, taxable income falls to 640,000 dollars and tax to 192,000 dollars. The project company pays 360,000 dollars of interest and has 448,000 dollars left for dividends, a total of 808,000 dollars flowing to the parent before any tax at the parent's end.

That 108,000 dollar difference is the reason thin capitalisation exists as a tax problem. But notice the word "before". The interest is income to the parent, may be taxed in the parent's country, and may suffer withholding tax when it crosses the border. Day 3 follows the money all the way home, and the advantage often shrinks.

Worked example two: the lender's view

Now add a senior construction lender. Suppose the bank will lend 60 percent of a 25,000,000 dollar project, 15,000,000 dollars, and requires 10,000,000 dollars of sponsor money. The sponsor wants to put in 4,000,000 dollars of shares and 6,000,000 dollars of shareholder loan.

The bank will almost always accept that, on conditions. The shareholder loan must be subordinated, meaning it is paid only after the senior loan, and it will be subject to a standstill, meaning the parent cannot demand repayment or enforce while the senior loan is outstanding. Many banks will count a subordinated shareholder loan as equity for their own sizing. What they will not accept is a shareholder loan that sits beside them, with security over the same building. So the form of your money must be designed with the bank's documents in mind, not after them.

How the best do it

Large institutional owners do not decide capitalisation project by project at the last minute. They keep a written funding policy: a target mix of shares and shareholder loans for each type of entity, a method for setting the interest rate, a standard loan agreement already reviewed by tax advisers in the relevant countries, and a rule that no money moves until the board of both lender and borrower has approved it. A small developer can copy this with a two-page funding policy and one template intercompany loan agreement, reviewed once and reused every time.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: interest deductibility, withholding and limits on interest all differ by country; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a shareholder loan can rank ahead of shares in insolvency, but courts in some systems can subordinate or recharacterise it. Banking: senior lenders will require subordination and a standstill, so draft the loan to fit. Governance: both boards approve the loan, and the minutes record the terms. Estate: an intercompany loan is an asset of the lending company and must appear in any estate or succession inventory. Exit: on a sale, the buyer will price the loan, and repaying it before or at closing is a separate decision with its own tax result.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in each country involved; corporate lawyer; the senior lender's counsel on subordination.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing by default: money moves without documents, and the label is applied later to whichever answer looks best. A tax authority, an auditor or a court then decides what it really was, using the facts you left behind. The control is a decision made and documented before the wire, with signed agreements and board minutes in both companies.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees the tax saving in Case B and puts as much in as debt as possible. He forgets the rules that cap interest, the withholding on the way out, the parent's own tax on the interest, and the bank that will subordinate the loan anyway. The saving is real only after all four.

Callback

In Week 37, Priya built the capital stack: senior debt, mezzanine, preferred and common equity, each with its priority. A shareholder loan is simply your own layer in that stack. The same questions apply, priority, security, cure rights and enforcement, except that you sit on both sides of the agreement, which is exactly why it has to be written down.

Recap

A parent can fund a project company with shares, loans or both. Loans can lower tax where the project is, rank ahead of shares and give a repayment schedule, but they are limited by tax rules, taxed on arrival and subordinated by banks. Choose the mix deliberately and document it before the money moves.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a loan that was never a loan.
checklist: I have decided the mix of shares and shareholder loan before any money moves.
Every intercompany loan has a signed agreement with amount, rate, repayment and default terms.
Both the lending and borrowing boards have approved the loan in minutes.
I have checked interest deductibility and interest limits in the project's country with a tax adviser.
I have checked withholding on interest and the parent's own tax on it.
The loan is drafted to accept the senior lender's subordination and standstill.
I have a written funding policy and a template loan agreement I reuse.
The loan appears in my estate and succession inventory.
head: Field checklist
speak: When my holding company funds a project company, it can do it as a shareholder or as a lender, and the form decides the cost. Shares carry no repayment date and no interest, and they are paid last. A shareholder loan carries a rate and a schedule, can rank ahead of shares, and its interest may be deductible where the project is. That is why people like it. But the saving is only real after four things: rules that cap interest, withholding when interest crosses a border, tax on the interest in the parent's country, and the senior bank, which will subordinate my loan and stop me enforcing it while its loan is outstanding. So I decide the mix before the money moves, I put it in a signed agreement approved by both boards, and I draft it to fit the bank's documents. A loan that exists only in a spreadsheet is whatever an auditor later decides it was.
terms: Capitalisation — the mix of share capital and debt, including shareholder loans, used to fund a company.
Thin capitalisation — funding a company mostly with debt from related parties and very little share capital, which many tax systems restrict.
Subordination — an agreement that one lender is paid only after another, usually the senior bank, is paid in full.

hostile.q: Your project company owes its own parent 6,000,000 dollars. Why should I treat that as anything other than equity dressed up to save tax?
hostile.a: Because it carries the terms an outside lender would require: a signed agreement, a market-tested rate, a repayment schedule, default provisions and board approvals in both companies, all dated before the money moved. The interest is being paid, or accrued under the agreement's terms, and recorded by both sides. It is subordinated to your loan by agreement, which is your protection, not a sign that it is not a loan. I can give you the agreement, the minutes and the rate analysis today.

title: The Loan That Was Never a Loan
summary: This is a composite example. A developer moved money from a holding company into a project company without documents, called it a loan when the tax return was due, and then watched a tax authority, an auditor and a bank each decide it was something else. Seven steps take it apart, ending in Rule 60.
body:
This is a composite example. Money moved between two companies the developer owned, nobody wrote down what it was, and three different outsiders later decided for him, each in the way that cost him most.

Recall

Q. What is subordination in a shareholder loan?

A. An agreement that the shareholder loan is paid only after the senior lender is paid in full, usually with a standstill that stops the shareholder enforcing while the senior loan is outstanding.

Q. What does withholding tax do on a cross-border payment?

A. It requires the payer to deduct tax from a payment such as interest or a dividend before it leaves the country, and remit it to the tax authority. Rates and exemptions vary and treaties may reduce them; verify against the primary source.

Q. What is bid levelling?

A. Adjusting competing bids to a common scope, so that exclusions, allowances and qualifications are priced in before they are compared.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me today because the evidence trail is the whole story. Nothing here was hidden or dishonest. It was simply undocumented, and an undocumented transaction between related companies is not neutral. It is a blank that the other side gets to fill in. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

Year 1: a developer's holding company in one country wires 5,000,000 dollars, in three tranches, to a new project company in another country to buy land and pay design fees. The bookkeeper records it in the project company as "due to parent". There is no agreement and no board resolution in either company. Year 2: the project company's accountant, preparing the first tax return, suggests treating the balance as a loan at 8 percent and accrues 400,000 dollars of interest as a deduction. Nothing is paid. Year 3: a construction lender's due diligence finds the balance, asks for the loan agreement and is given one, drafted that month and dated back to year 1. Year 4: the tax authority audits. It concludes the advance was equity, denies three years of interest deductions and assesses tax, interest and a penalty. The lender's counsel learns the agreement was backdated and the relationship with the bank is damaged.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Wiring money before deciding what it was. Choosing the label at tax time, to fit the answer that saved most tax. And producing a document after the fact, dated earlier than it was signed, to satisfy the lender.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed that because he owned both companies, the label was his to choose whenever he liked. He assumed an accrued interest deduction would be accepted because the rate looked reasonable. And he assumed a document could be produced later if anyone asked.

4. Incentives

The accountant was paid to lower the year 2 tax bill and had no responsibility for the bank's diligence. The developer was rewarded in the short run for speed: land bought quickly, design started. Nobody in the chain was paid to think about how the advance would look in year 4, to a stranger, with the documents on the table.

5. Warning signs ignored

No interest was ever paid, and no repayment schedule existed. The rate was chosen at tax time rather than at the time of the advance. The balance had no maturity and no security. The project company had almost no share capital, so the loan was the entire funding. And the lender asked for a document that should already have existed. Each of these is a factor that tax authorities and courts in many systems weigh when deciding whether something is really debt.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the backdated agreement. Up to then, the problem was one of characterisation: an argument about what an undocumented advance had been, which a well-advised developer might have resolved by conceding it was equity and paying the tax. Once a document was dated to a time it did not exist, the problem became one of credibility, with the tax authority and with the bank. Cole's view is blunt: a backdated document can turn a tax dispute into something far more serious, and in many systems it may carry consequences beyond tax. Professional sign-off required: lawyer, the moment anyone suggests dating a document earlier than it was signed.

7. Root cause

The root cause was money moving between related companies with no decision recorded at the time. Every later mistake, the label at tax time, the unpaid interest, the backdated agreement, was an attempt to fill that blank after the fact. The tax authority, the auditor and the bank all applied the same principle: what the parties actually did at the time outweighs what they called it later.

What a good outcome looked like

Before the first wire, the developer decides: 1,000,000 dollars as shares, 4,000,000 dollars as a loan. Both boards approve. A template intercompany loan agreement is signed with a rate supported by a short written analysis of what an unrelated lender would charge, a maturity, a repayment schedule, and a clause anticipating subordination to a future senior lender. Interest is paid or accrued exactly as the agreement says, and both companies record it the same way. When the bank asks, the file is ready in an hour. When the tax authority asks, the argument is about the rate, not about whether a loan existed.

Cole's evidence list

When an auditor or tax inspector tests whether an intercompany balance is really a loan, Cole says they ask for six things, and you should be able to hand over each one. First, the signed agreement, dated when it was signed. Second, the board resolutions in both companies approving it. Third, the bank records showing when and how much money moved, matched to the agreement. Fourth, evidence that interest was paid or accrued exactly as agreed, in both sets of books. Fifth, a note made at the time explaining why the rate was reasonable, for example quotes or published rates for similar loans to unrelated borrowers. Sixth, evidence that the borrower could plausibly repay: a projection showing the project generating cash to service the loan. Missing any one of these does not prove the loan false. Missing all six, as in this case, leaves almost nothing to argue with.

Say that out loud now.

Rule 60

Rule 60: Never move money between your own companies until a signed agreement and board approvals in both companies say what it is, on terms a stranger would accept; and never date a document earlier than the day it was signed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the shortcut feels harmless because you own both sides. The control is the rule above, made automatic: your bank signatory mandate in the holding company requires an approved intercompany agreement number before any transfer to an affiliate is released.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the danger is the interest rate. It is not. The danger is the absence of any record at the time, which lets someone else decide what the money was.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught that an adviser can only advise on the facts you give them, and that an engagement letter defines what they were asked. Here the accountant was asked a narrow question, how to lower one year's tax, and answered it. Nobody asked the wider question, what is this advance and how will it be read in four years, because nobody was engaged to answer it.

Recap

An undocumented advance between related companies was labelled a loan at tax time, never serviced, and backed by a document dated after the fact. A tax authority treated it as equity, and the bank lost confidence. Rule 60 fixes the decision before the wire and forbids backdating.

Next: Nadia on The Money: what the funding mix does to after-tax return and to the senior lender's coverage.
checklist: No transfer to an affiliate leaves without a signed agreement reference.
Both boards approve every intercompany loan before funding.
The rate is supported by a written analysis made at the time.
Interest is paid or accrued exactly as the agreement states.
Both companies record the loan and interest identically.
The loan anticipates subordination to a future senior lender.
No document is ever dated earlier than the day it was signed.
I keep the intercompany file ready for a lender or auditor within an hour.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. A developer wired five million dollars from his holding company to a project company with no agreement and no board approval. At tax time his accountant called it a loan and deducted interest that was never paid. When a bank asked for the loan agreement, one was drafted and dated back two years. The tax authority later decided the money was equity and denied the deductions with penalties, and the bank lost trust when it learned the document was backdated. The root cause was not the interest rate. It was money moving between related companies with nothing recorded at the time, which let three outsiders decide what it was. Rule 60: never move money between your own companies until a signed agreement and board approvals say what it is, on terms a stranger would accept, and never date a document earlier than the day it was signed.
terms: Characterisation — the decision, by a tax authority, auditor or court, about what a transaction legally is, regardless of its label.
Backdating — dating a document earlier than the day it was actually signed, which can destroy credibility and may carry legal consequences.
Advance — a transfer of money from one company to another before its legal nature, loan or share capital, has been fixed.

hostile.q: This loan agreement is dated three years ago. When was it actually signed?
hostile.a: It was signed on the date shown on it, and here are the board minutes from both companies on that same date and the bank records of the first transfer three days later. If any of our documents had been signed later, I would tell you so, give you the actual date, and describe it as a later confirmation of an earlier arrangement, never as the original.

rule: Rule 60: Never move money between your own companies until a signed agreement and board approvals in both companies say what it is, on terms a stranger would accept; and never date a document earlier than the day it was signed.

title: Following the Dollar Home: Funding Mix, After-Tax Cash and Coverage
summary: The tax saving from a shareholder loan looks large inside the project company and shrinks on the way home. This lesson follows one year of cash from the project to the parent under two funding mixes, then shows how the senior lender treats your loan in its coverage test.
body:
The only number that matters is the after-tax cash that reaches the parent; a saving measured inside the project company is half an answer, and the other half is usually smaller than you hoped.

Recall

Q. Why is a backdated intercompany agreement so damaging?

A. Because it turns an argument about what an advance was into a question of credibility with the tax authority and the bank, and in many systems it may carry consequences beyond tax.

Q. What is leakage in repatriation?

A. The tax and cost lost between profit earned in the project company and cash arriving in the owner's hands: local tax, withholding, tax at the parent's end, and transaction costs.

Q. What does a schedule of values do?

A. It breaks the contract sum into line items that the contractor bills against, so each payment application can be checked against work in place.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in Day 1 Omar showed a 108,000 dollar saving from funding with a shareholder loan. That figure was measured at the wrong place. Your wealth is built from cash that reaches you, after every tax on the route. Today we follow the dollar all the way home, then look at the same loan through the senior lender's eyes.

The route home

Plain English. Each dollar of project profit can come home as a dividend or as interest on your shareholder loan. A dividend is paid from after-tax profit, then may suffer withholding tax as it leaves the country, then may or may not be taxed again where the parent is. Interest is deducted before project tax, then may suffer withholding, then is usually taxed as ordinary income at the parent's end, perhaps with a credit for the withholding. The professional framing is an effective tax rate: total tax on the route, divided by the pre-tax profit.

Every rate below is hypothetical, chosen for arithmetic and taken from no country: project-country tax 30 percent; withholding of 15 percent on dividends and 10 percent on interest; parent-country tax of 25 percent on interest income, with a credit for withholding; dividends received by the parent exempt. Verify every real rate and every credit rule against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example one: two mixes, one year

The project earns 1,000,000 dollars before interest and tax.

Case A, all shares. Project tax is 300,000 dollars. The dividend is 700,000 dollars. Withholding at 15 percent is 105,000 dollars. The parent receives 595,000 dollars, exempt at home. Cash home: 595,000 dollars. Effective rate: 40.5 percent.

Case B, 6,000,000 dollars of loan at 6 percent. Interest is 360,000 dollars, leaving 640,000 dollars of taxable profit, project tax of 192,000 dollars and a dividend of 448,000 dollars. On the dividend: withholding of 67,200 dollars, so 380,800 dollars arrives, exempt. On the interest: withholding of 36,000 dollars, so 324,000 dollars arrives. Parent tax on interest is 25 percent of 360,000, which is 90,000 dollars, less the 36,000 dollar credit, so 54,000 dollars is payable. Net interest home is 270,000 dollars. Cash home: 380,800 plus 270,000, which is 650,800 dollars. Effective rate: 34.9 percent.

The saving is 55,800 dollars, about half of the 108,000 dollars Omar measured inside the project. Change one hypothetical assumption, for example a parent country that taxes interest at a higher rate or gives no credit for withholding, and the saving can disappear or reverse. That is why the comparison is always run end to end.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: what the senior lender sees

Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) is net operating income divided by debt service, the year's scheduled interest and principal. Suppose the stabilised building earns NOI of 1,000,000 dollars and senior debt service is 700,000 dollars. DSCR is 1,000,000 divided by 700,000, or 1.43 times.

If the bank counted your shareholder loan interest of 360,000 dollars as debt service, coverage would be 1,000,000 divided by 1,060,000, or 0.94 times, which would fail almost any covenant. Most banks therefore do not count it, because the shareholder loan is subordinated and paid only from cash left after senior debt service. But the price of that treatment is control: the bank's distribution test, often a minimum DSCR and no default, decides whether your interest can be paid at all. In a weak year the shareholder interest accrues and the cash stays in the project. Your tax plan assumed the interest was paid; your bank decides whether it is. Model both.

Worked example three: the principal at refinancing

The larger effect is often not the annual interest but the principal. Suppose that after stabilisation the project refinances and has 5,000,000 dollars of surplus cash to send home. If the parent funded with shares, sending that cash home is usually a dividend or a return of capital, and which one it is depends on local company and tax law. Treated as a dividend at the hypothetical 15 percent withholding, 750,000 dollars stays behind. If instead the parent had lent 5,000,000 dollars, repaying the loan principal is usually not income at all, so in most systems no withholding applies and the full 5,000,000 dollars arrives. A return of share capital may achieve a similar result, but it often needs formal steps under company law, such as a solvency test and a shareholder resolution. Verify each of these against the primary source before you rely on it.

The lesson is that the funding mix decides not only the yearly leakage but the cost of getting your original money back. Run the exit year in the model, not only a stabilised year.

Timing and the books

Nadia's accounting point: in the project company the loan is a liability and accrued interest is an expense; in the parent the loan is a receivable and the interest is income. The two sets of books must match to the dollar every period, and the auditor will reconcile them. Where interest accrues but is not paid, some systems restrict the deduction until payment, or treat unpaid related-party interest differently; verify against the primary source.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's view for your personal balance sheet: a shareholder loan in your holding company looks like a receivable, a near-cash asset. It is not. While a senior loan is outstanding, it is subordinated and frozen by a standstill, so its liquidity is close to that of the shares beside it. Record it in your liquidity tiers with the shares, not with your cash reserve, and count it toward your concentration in that one project. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal tax or investment decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is deciding the funding mix on the project-level saving alone. The control is an end-to-end model, prepared with tax advisers in both countries, that follows one year of cash from project profit to the parent under each mix, and a second run in which the bank blocks distributions.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes interest on his shareholder loan will be paid on schedule because he controls both companies. The senior lender's distribution test controls it, not him.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage and Elias warned about after-tax leakage: a pre-tax internal rate of return (IRR) can look excellent while the investor's after-tax return is ordinary. This lesson is the same warning applied to the structure's own plumbing. Measure where the cash lands, not where it starts.

Recap

A shareholder loan saves project tax, but withholding and parent-country tax take back part of it, sometimes all of it. The senior lender excludes your interest from coverage only because it controls whether that interest is paid. Model the route end to end, and model the blocked year.

Next: Elias on The Rules: thin capitalisation, interest limits and how tax authorities test whether debt is really debt.
checklist: I have modelled after-tax cash to the parent, not just project-level tax.
I have run the comparison under each funding mix with tax advisers in both countries.
I know the withholding on interest and on dividends and whether a treaty reduces it.
I know whether the parent country gives a credit for withholding.
I know how my senior lender treats shareholder loan interest in its coverage test.
I have modelled a year in which distributions are blocked and interest accrues.
Both companies' books reconcile the loan and interest every period.
My shareholder loan sits in my illiquid tier, not my cash reserve.
head: Field checklist
speak: The tax saving from a shareholder loan is usually measured inside the project company, and that is the wrong place. In my hypothetical, a six million dollar loan saved 108,000 dollars of project tax. Following the cash home, withholding on the interest and tax on it at the parent's end took back about half, leaving roughly 56,000 dollars. Change one assumption and the saving can vanish. So I always model one year of cash from project profit to the parent under each mix. Then I look through the bank's eyes. The bank leaves my shareholder interest out of its coverage ratio only because my loan is subordinated, which means its distribution test decides whether that interest is paid at all. In a weak year it accrues and the cash stays put. On my personal balance sheet, that loan is illiquid, not cash.
terms: Effective tax rate — total tax paid on the route from profit to owner, divided by the pre-tax profit.
Distribution test — a loan condition, often a minimum coverage ratio and no default, that must be met before cash may be paid to owners or shareholder lenders.
Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) — net operating income divided by scheduled interest and principal for the period.

hostile.q: Your model shows shareholder interest paid every year. My distribution test would have blocked it in years 2 and 3. Which number is right?
hostile.a: Yours. I have rerun the model with your distribution test applied: in years 2 and 3 the interest accrues, cash is retained in the project, and the parent's after-tax cash falls in those years. I have also checked with our tax advisers how unpaid related-party interest is treated in the project's country, and the model reflects that. I would rather plan on your test than discover it.

title: Thin Capitalisation and Interest Limits: How the Rules Push Back
summary: Because related-party interest can move profit from one country to another, tax systems restrict it. This lesson teaches the four families of rules, ratio tests, earnings tests, arm's-length tests and recharacterisation, and the facts that decide whether debt is treated as debt.
body:
Every tax system knows that a parent can lend to its own subsidiary to move profit across a border, so every serious system has rules that limit how much related-party interest it will allow, and you plan inside those limits or you plan to be reassessed.

Recall

Q. Why is the saving from a shareholder loan smaller at the parent than in the project company?

A. Because withholding tax on the interest and tax on the interest income at the parent's end take back part of the project-level saving.

Q. What is a tie-breaker rule in a tax treaty?

A. A rule that decides which country a person or company is resident in for treaty purposes when both countries' domestic laws claim it, often by looking at where effective management sits.

Q. What is the difference between construction management at risk and construction management as agent?

A. At risk, the construction manager holds the trade contracts and usually guarantees a maximum price. As agent, it advises the owner, who holds the trade contracts and carries the cost risk.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I teach these rules as concepts. Every country writes them differently, changes them often, and the details decide the answer. Nothing here is a statement of any country's law; verify each point against the primary source before you rely on it. What I can give you is the map, so you know which questions to ask your advisers and why their answers differ between countries.

The four families of rules

First, ratio tests. The rule caps related-party debt at a multiple of the company's equity. Interest on debt above the cap is not deductible, and in some systems the excess interest is treated as a dividend, with dividend withholding. This is the classic thin capitalisation rule.

Second, earnings tests. The rule caps net interest deductions at a percentage of a measure of earnings, often earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Many countries have moved toward this approach following international work on base erosion, and some apply it to all interest, not only related-party interest. Some allow denied interest to be carried forward to later years. Every percentage, threshold and carry rule must be verified against the primary source.

Third, arm's-length tests. The rule asks whether an unrelated lender would have lent this amount, at this rate, on these terms, to this borrower. If not, the excess amount or the excess interest is disallowed. This overlaps with transfer pricing, which Cole teaches next week.

Fourth, recharacterisation. Rather than capping the interest, the authority decides the instrument was never debt and treats the whole advance as share capital. Payments called interest then become dividends. That is what happened in Day 2.

Say that out loud now.

When is debt really debt?

Courts and tax authorities in common-law countries tend to weigh a recurring set of facts. None is decisive alone; they are weighed together. Is there a written agreement made at the time? Is there a fixed maturity and a repayment schedule? Is interest payable regardless of profit, and was it actually paid? Is there security or, at least, a right to sue for repayment? Did the borrower have a realistic ability to repay from its own cash flow? Would an outside lender have lent on similar terms? How large is the debt compared with the share capital? And did the parties treat it as debt in their books, their minutes and their dealings with others?

Subordination to a senior bank is common and is not usually fatal on its own, because outside mezzanine lenders accept subordination too. But a loan that is subordinated, unsecured, interest-free, with no maturity and no repayment ever made, looks much more like equity than like debt.

Worked example one: a ratio test

Suppose a hypothetical rule allows related-party debt up to 1.5 times equity. These numbers are illustrations, not any country's rule. The project company has 4,000,000 dollars of share capital and 8,000,000 dollars of shareholder loan at 6 percent, so interest is 480,000 dollars.

Allowed debt is 1.5 times 4,000,000, which is 6,000,000 dollars. The excess is 2,000,000 dollars, a quarter of the loan. So a quarter of the interest, 120,000 dollars, is denied, and 360,000 dollars is deductible. If this hypothetical rule also treats denied interest as a dividend, the 120,000 dollars may attract dividend withholding instead of interest withholding. The fix, if the numbers matter, is to convert 2,000,000 dollars of loan into shares before the year in question, with proper resolutions in both companies.

Worked example two: an earnings test

Now suppose a hypothetical rule limits net interest to 30 percent of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The stabilised project has such earnings of 1,000,000 dollars, a senior bank loan with 500,000 dollars of interest and a shareholder loan with 360,000 dollars of interest, a total of 860,000 dollars.

The cap is 300,000 dollars. In this hypothetical, 560,000 dollars of interest is denied, including much of the senior bank's interest, because this type of rule usually caps all interest, not only related-party interest. During construction, when earnings are zero, the cap may be zero, and everything depends on whether denied interest carries forward and whether construction interest is added to the cost of the building instead. A shareholder loan that looked efficient can add nothing at all under an earnings test.

Withholding, treaties and anti-hybrid rules

Two further rules sit beside these. Withholding on interest may be reduced by a tax treaty, but only for a lender that is the beneficial owner of the interest, as Week 57 taught. And anti-hybrid rules deny a deduction where the same payment is deductible in one country and not taxed in the other, for example because the instrument is debt in one country and equity in the other. Ask your advisers whether your instrument is characterised the same way in both countries.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in the project's country and in the parent's country, reviewing the instrument together, not separately.

The order of the questions

In practice your advisers should ask the questions in a fixed order, because each one can make the next irrelevant. First: is this instrument debt at all, on the facts? If it is equity, nothing else matters. Second: is the amount within any ratio test? Third: is the rate within an arm's-length range? Fourth: after the first three, is total net interest within any earnings test this year, and if not, what carries forward? Fifth: what withholding applies when the interest is paid, and does a treaty reduce it? Sixth: how is the same payment treated in the parent's country? Write the answers on one page for each loan, dated and signed by the adviser, and refresh it every year. That page is what you hand an auditor, and it is what protects you when the rules change between funding and exit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is planning under one family of rules and being tested under another, for example sizing the loan to a ratio test in a country that has since moved to an earnings test. The control is an annual review of interest-limitation rules in each country, recorded in the tax file, before the year's funding decisions.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks the rate and forgets the amount. A perfectly market rate on far too much related-party debt can still be denied.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught substance over form: the authority looks at what was actually done, not at what it was called. Thin capitalisation and recharacterisation are substance over form applied to money. A loan is debt because of how it behaves, not because a ledger calls it one.

Recap

Four families of rules limit related-party interest: ratio tests, earnings tests, arm's-length tests and recharacterisation. The facts that make debt real are a contemporaneous agreement, maturity, interest actually paid, ability to repay and consistent treatment. Plan inside the rules of both countries.

Next: Nadia on The Numbers: reverse engineering the largest shareholder loan the rules and the bank will allow.
checklist: I know whether the project's country uses a ratio test, an earnings test, or both.
I know whether the cap applies to all interest or only related-party interest.
I know whether denied interest carries forward and how construction interest is treated.
My loan has the features of real debt: agreement, maturity, schedule, paid interest.
I have checked whether denied interest is treated as a dividend.
I have confirmed the instrument is characterised the same way in both countries.
Treaty-reduced withholding is claimed only by the beneficial owner.
The interest-limitation rules are reviewed every year before funding decisions.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every tax system knows a parent can lend to its own subsidiary to move profit, so every serious system limits it. There are four families of rules. Ratio tests cap related-party debt at a multiple of equity. Earnings tests cap net interest at a percentage of earnings, and often apply to all interest, including the bank's. Arm's-length tests ask whether an outside lender would have lent this amount at this rate. Recharacterisation treats the whole loan as share capital, so the interest becomes a dividend. What makes debt real is behaviour: a written agreement at the time, a maturity, interest that is actually paid, a borrower able to repay, and both companies treating it as debt. Under an earnings test, a project with no earnings during construction may get no deduction at all. So I plan inside both countries' rules, reviewed every year, with advisers from both countries in the same conversation.
terms: Ratio test — a thin capitalisation rule capping related-party debt at a multiple of the company's equity.
Earnings test — a rule capping net interest deductions at a percentage of a measure of the company's earnings.
Recharacterisation — treating an instrument as something other than its label, for example treating a loan as share capital.

hostile.q: Your related-party debt is twice your equity and the interest has never been paid. Why shouldn't I recharacterise the whole advance as share capital?
hostile.a: Because the other factors point the other way, and I can show you each one: a signed agreement from the day of funding, board approvals in both companies, a fixed maturity, a rate supported by evidence of what unrelated lenders charged, and a projection showing repayment from refinancing. The interest has accrued rather than been paid because the senior lender's distribution test blocked payment, and here is that clause. I accept that interest above any allowed ratio is not deductible, and our return already excludes it.

title: Reverse Engineering the Largest Shareholder Loan That Works
summary: Start from the outcome you want, a deductible interest stream the bank will let you receive, and work backward through four limits to the largest shareholder loan that survives all of them. The smallest answer wins, exactly as in debt sizing.
body:
A shareholder loan is sized like a bank loan: compute the maximum under every limit that applies, and the smallest answer is the loan, because the binding limit is the only one that matters.

Recall

Q. Name the four families of interest-limitation rules.

A. Ratio tests, earnings tests, arm's-length tests and recharacterisation.

Q. What is a controlled foreign company rule trying to prevent?

A. Passive income being accumulated in a foreign company the owner controls, untaxed at home until distributed. Many such rules tax it at home as it arises; verify the detail against the primary source.

Q. In bank debt sizing, what is the binding limit?

A. The smallest of the loan amounts produced by each test, such as loan-to-cost, loan-to-value and debt service coverage. The lender lends the smallest.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Week 36 taught you to size a bank loan by running every test and taking the smallest. Today we use the same discipline on your own loan to your own project company. The instinct is to choose the loan amount first and test it afterwards. Reverse the order. Start from the outcome you want, then work backward through every limit, and let the numbers choose the amount. Every figure and every rule here is hypothetical, chosen for arithmetic and taken from no country. Verify every real rule against the primary source before you rely on it.

The outcome we start from

The parent has committed 10,000,000 dollars of sponsor money to a project. The outcome it wants is a shareholder loan whose interest is fully deductible in the project's country every year after stabilisation, and which the senior bank will let the project actually pay. We need the largest loan that delivers that outcome.

The project's stabilised figures: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of 1,200,000 dollars a year. Senior bank loan interest of 200,000 dollars a year and principal of 600,000 dollars a year, so senior debt service is 800,000 dollars. For simplicity, treat net operating income as equal to those earnings, 1,200,000 dollars.

The hypothetical rules: a ratio test allowing related-party debt up to 1.5 times equity; an earnings test capping all net interest at 30 percent of those earnings; an arm's-length interest rate of 6 percent, supported by evidence; and a bank distribution test requiring senior coverage of at least 1.25 times before any payment to shareholders.

Step 1: the ratio limit

Let L be the loan. Equity is then 10,000,000 minus L. The test requires L to be no more than 1.5 times equity.

L is at most 1.5 times (10,000,000 minus L). Expand: L is at most 15,000,000 minus 1.5L. Add 1.5L to both sides: 2.5L is at most 15,000,000. Divide by 2.5: L is at most 6,000,000 dollars.

Ratio limit: 6,000,000 dollars of loan, 4,000,000 dollars of shares.

Step 2: the earnings limit

The cap on all net interest is 30 percent of 1,200,000 dollars, which is 360,000 dollars a year. The senior bank already uses 200,000 dollars of it. The room left for shareholder interest is 360,000 minus 200,000, which is 160,000 dollars a year.

At the 6 percent rate, the loan that produces 160,000 dollars of interest is 160,000 divided by 0.06, which is 2,666,667 dollars. Round down to 2,650,000 dollars to leave a margin for small changes in earnings.

Earnings limit: about 2,650,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: the bank's distribution limit

Senior coverage is 1,200,000 divided by 800,000, which is 1.5 times. That passes the 1.25 times test, so distributions are allowed. The cash left after senior debt service is 1,200,000 minus 800,000, which is 400,000 dollars, before tax. Shareholder interest of 159,000 dollars, on 2,650,000 dollars at 6 percent, fits comfortably inside it.

Now ask how far earnings can fall before the bank blocks payment. Coverage of 1.25 times on 800,000 dollars needs earnings of 1,000,000 dollars. So a fall of 200,000 dollars, about 17 percent, stops the interest. Note that same fall also cuts the earnings cap to 300,000 dollars, leaving only 100,000 dollars of room. In a weak year, the interest is both blocked by the bank and partly non-deductible. Record that as the trigger to watch.

Step 4: the rate check

The rate must be defensible as arm's length. If the evidence supported a range from 5 to 7 percent, choosing 7 percent would shrink the loan the earnings test allows: 160,000 divided by 0.07 is about 2,285,714 dollars. A higher rate does not buy more deduction here, because the binding limit is the dollar cap on interest, not the loan amount. So 6 percent, the middle of the supported range, is both the more defensible rate and the one that does not reduce the loan.

The answer

Limits: ratio 6,000,000 dollars; earnings about 2,650,000 dollars; bank distribution comfortably satisfied at the stabilised figures. The binding limit is the earnings test. The structure is about 2,650,000 dollars of shareholder loan and 7,350,000 dollars of shares.

Notice what the reverse method prevented. A developer who started from the ratio test would have lent 6,000,000 dollars and found that more than half the interest was never deductible.

Step 5: what the answer means in the documents

The number has to become paper before any money moves. The project company issues 7,350,000 dollars of shares to the parent, recorded in its share register and approved by its board. The parent and the project company sign a 2,650,000 dollar loan agreement at 6 percent, with a maturity, a repayment schedule tied to the expected refinancing, and a clause accepting subordination to the senior lender. The parent's board approves the loan as lender, the project company's board as borrower. The sizing sheet, the rate evidence and the adviser's note go into the intercompany file with the same date.

Then set a review date. If stabilised earnings come in at 1,500,000 dollars rather than 1,200,000 dollars, the earnings cap rises to 450,000 dollars, the room to 250,000 dollars, and the loan the test supports to about 4,166,667 dollars. Increasing a shareholder loan later is possible, with new resolutions and a new agreement, but it must be a fresh, dated decision, never a quiet change to an old file.

A second check: the years before stabilisation

Earnings during construction are zero, so the earnings cap is zero and no interest is deductible in those years unless the local rules add it to the cost of the building or carry it forward. Ask your adviser both questions, and model the shareholder interest during construction as accruing without any current deduction until they answer. In many deals that single fact changes the answer more than all four steps above.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in the project's country on every rule used here; the senior lender's counsel on the distribution test.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing the loan to the most generous rule and ignoring the binding one. The control is a one-page sizing sheet, like a bank's, listing every limit, its result and which one binds, refreshed whenever earnings forecasts or the rules change.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner raises the interest rate to get more deduction. When the binding limit is a dollar cap on interest, a higher rate only shrinks the loan the cap allows, while making the rate harder to defend.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught break-evens and triggers: find the point at which a plan fails and watch for it. Step 3 found one: a 17 percent fall in earnings blocks the shareholder interest and cuts its deductibility at the same time. That number belongs on the project's trigger list beside the bank's covenants.

Recap

Start from the outcome, a deductible interest stream the bank lets you receive, and work backward through the ratio test, the earnings test, the bank's distribution test and the rate check. The smallest result is the loan. Here the earnings test bound at about 2,650,000 dollars.

Next: Omar on The Room: the meeting where the senior lender's counsel and your auditor both ask about the shareholder loan.
checklist: I size the shareholder loan from the outcome backward, not from a chosen amount.
I compute the ratio limit, the earnings limit and the bank's distribution limit.
I take the smallest result as the loan and record which limit binds.
I choose a rate inside a documented arm's-length range.
I know how far earnings can fall before the bank blocks shareholder interest.
I know how interest is treated during construction, when earnings are zero.
I keep a one-page sizing sheet and refresh it when forecasts or rules change.
A tax adviser in the project's country has confirmed every rule I used.
head: Field checklist
speak: I size my own shareholder loan the way a bank sizes its loan: every limit, then the smallest. Here the parent had ten million dollars to put in. A hypothetical ratio test allowed six million of loan. A hypothetical earnings test capped all interest at 360,000 dollars, and the bank's interest used 200,000 of that, leaving 160,000. At a six percent arm's-length rate, that supports about 2.65 million dollars of loan. The bank's distribution test passed, but a 17 percent fall in earnings would block the interest and cut the deductible room at the same time, so that is a trigger I watch. A higher rate would not help, because the cap is in dollars. So the loan is about 2.65 million, and the rest goes in as shares. Starting from the ratio test would have produced a loan whose interest was mostly never deductible.
terms: Binding limit — the smallest result among all the tests that apply, which therefore sets the actual amount.
Earnings room — the portion of an earnings-based interest cap not already used by other interest.
Sizing sheet — a one-page record listing each limit, its result and which one binds.

hostile.q: Why is your shareholder loan only 2,650,000 dollars when the ratio rule would allow 6,000,000?
hostile.a: Because the ratio rule is not the binding limit. The earnings-based cap on all interest leaves about 160,000 dollars of room after the senior loan's interest, which supports about 2,650,000 dollars at our documented rate. Lending more would create interest we could not deduct. I have the sizing sheet showing each limit and which one binds.

title: The Shareholder Loan on the Table: Lender's Counsel and the Auditor
summary: A scene before a construction loan closes, where the senior lender's counsel wants your shareholder loan subordinated and frozen, and the project company's auditor wants evidence that it is a loan at all. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, and the question behind each question.
body:
In the room where your own loan is examined, you win by having already decided what it is and by being able to prove it, not by arguing for the most favourable label.

Recall

Q. In the reverse-engineered sizing, why did a higher interest rate not increase the deduction?

A. Because the binding limit was an earnings-based dollar cap on interest. A higher rate only shrinks the loan the cap allows.

Q. What is beneficial ownership in a treaty claim?

A. The requirement that the person claiming reduced withholding is the one truly entitled to the income, not a conduit passing it on to someone else.

Q. What is the purpose of prequalification in procurement?

A. To screen bidders for financial strength, experience, safety and capacity before they price, so the lowest bid comes from a firm able to deliver.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two very different people will examine your shareholder loan, often in the same week. The senior lender's counsel wants your loan to be harmless to the bank: subordinated, unsecured or second-ranking, and frozen until the bank is repaid. The auditor wants to know whether it is really a loan, because that decides how the books and the tax return are prepared. Each wants something that looks, at first, like the opposite of what the other wants. They are not opposed, and the person who understands that runs the meeting.

The scene

This is a hypothetical scene. A video call two weeks before a 15,000,000 dollar construction loan closes. On the call: the bank's counsel, the project company's auditor, your corporate lawyer and you. The project company has 7,350,000 dollars of shares and a 2,650,000 dollar shareholder loan, documented as in Day 5.

The bank's counsel opens: "We will need the shareholder loan fully subordinated, with a standstill on enforcement, no payments while any default is continuing, and no payments at all unless our distribution test is met. We would also like an assignment of the loan to us as security."

The auditor then asks: "If the shareholder loan cannot be repaid until the bank is paid, and interest can be blocked indefinitely, how is this different from equity?"

The lines to say

To the bank's counsel: "We expected subordination and a standstill, and the loan agreement already provides for them. We accept no payments during a continuing default and the distribution test as drafted in your term sheet. On the assignment as security, we can agree, provided it is released when your loan is repaid."

To the auditor: "Subordination changes when the loan is paid, not whether it is owed. The agreement has a maturity, a rate supported by evidence, and a repayment schedule tied to refinancing. Mezzanine lenders who are strangers to us accept subordination on the same terms. Here is the agreement, both boards' resolutions, the rate analysis and the sizing sheet, all dated before the funds moved."

Then to both: "Can we agree the subordination wording now, so the auditor can review the final form before closing?"

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say "it's whatever works best for tax." It tells the auditor the label is negotiable, which is exactly what makes recharacterisation likely.

Never say "it's really equity, so don't worry about it" to the bank, and "it's really a loan" to the auditor in the next breath. Both are on the call, and even when they are not, documents travel.

Never say "we can paper that afterwards." Day 2 showed where that ends.

Never say "we'll just repay the shareholder loan first from the construction draws." Using the bank's money to repay your own loan is almost always prohibited, and suggesting it marks you as a sponsor who needs watching.

The question behind the question

Behind the bank counsel's demands is one question: if this project goes wrong, can the sponsor's loan compete with ours for the building? Every clause they ask for answers that. Once you see it, you can concede the substance quickly and negotiate only the edges, such as the release of the assignment.

Behind the auditor's question is a different one: can I sign off these accounts, and the tax treatment in them, on the evidence you have given me? The auditor is not trying to deny your deduction. The auditor is trying not to be wrong. Give them evidence, not arguments.

When to stay silent

After you hand over the evidence file, stop. The auditor will need to read it. Filling the silence with reasons why the loan is commercially sensible adds nothing and invites a new question. Likewise, when the bank's counsel lists their demands, let them finish the list before you respond. Interrupting after the first item means negotiating against an incomplete picture.

How to hold your state

A meeting where two professionals examine your own transaction can feel like an accusation. It is not. It is the ordinary price of borrowing someone else's money and of having audited accounts. Keep your voice low and slow, answer in short sentences, and use the phrase from Week 6 when you do not know: "I'll confirm that with our tax adviser and come back to you by Friday." Breathing drills are for after the call, seated, not during it, and check them with your doctor if you have any condition that might be affected.

What to send after the call

Within one working day, send a short email to everyone on the call. One paragraph confirms what was agreed: subordination and standstill on the bank's wording, no payments during a continuing default, payments only when the distribution test is met, and an assignment released on repayment. A second paragraph lists what the auditor asked for and the date each item will arrive. A third names any open point, with the person responsible and the date. Attach nothing you did not discuss. This email becomes a contemporaneous record, the kind Vera insists on: a note made at the time of what was decided and by whom. It also protects you if, months later, someone remembers the meeting differently. Keep it plain, keep it factual, and send it before memories start to drift.

A second version of the scene

Suppose the loan had not been documented. The auditor asks the same question, and there is no file. The honest line is: "The advances were not documented as a loan at the time. We have taken advice, and we propose to treat them as share capital from the date they were made. Here is the corporate lawyer's note and the board resolution confirming that." That line may cost tax. It costs far less than the alternative in Day 2, and it preserves your credibility with both people on the call.

Professional sign-off required: corporate lawyer, on the subordination agreement; tax adviser, on the characterisation; the auditor, on the accounting.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in this room is telling each party what it wants to hear. The control is one set of documents and one story, prepared before the meeting, that you would be comfortable having read aloud to both at once.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner fights the subordination, treating it as a loss. Banks lend on the basis that your money is behind theirs; fighting it signals that you misunderstand the deal, and wins nothing.

Callback

In Week 37, Priya taught intercreditor agreements between a senior lender and a mezzanine lender: payment priority, cure rights and limits on enforcement. The subordination agreement for your shareholder loan is the same document with a friendlier counterparty. Read it with the same care, because in a default you will want the same rights a mezzanine lender would.

Recap

The bank wants your loan unable to compete with its own; the auditor wants evidence the loan is real. Concede subordination, prove reality with documents made at the time, keep one story for both, and stay silent while the evidence is read.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair on a hypothetical intercompany loan agreement.
checklist: I know the subordination terms the bank will ask for before the meeting.
My loan agreement already provides for subordination and a standstill.
I have one evidence file ready for the auditor, dated before funding.
I tell the bank and the auditor the same story.
I never propose repaying my own loan from construction draws.
I let each party finish its list before I respond.
I use 'I'll confirm by Friday' rather than guessing.
If the loan was not documented, I disclose it and treat it as share capital on advice.
head: Field checklist
speak: Before a construction loan closes, two people examine my shareholder loan. The bank's counsel wants it subordinated, frozen while the bank is owed, and payable only when the distribution test is met. The auditor wants to know whether it is a loan at all. Those demands only look opposed. Subordination changes when my loan is paid, not whether it is owed, and stranger mezzanine lenders accept the same terms. So I concede the substance to the bank quickly, negotiate the edges such as releasing any assignment, and give the auditor evidence: the agreement, both boards' resolutions, the rate analysis and the sizing sheet, all dated before the money moved. I tell both the same story, I never suggest repaying my loan from construction draws, and after I hand over the file I stop talking. If the loan was never documented, I say so and treat it as share capital.
terms: Standstill — a promise by a junior lender not to demand repayment or enforce its rights for a set period, usually while the senior loan is outstanding.
Assignment as security — a transfer of the benefit of a contract, such as a shareholder loan, to a lender as collateral for its own loan.
Evidence file — the dated set of documents proving what a transaction was at the time it was made.

hostile.q: If we block your interest whenever the distribution test fails, and you cannot enforce until we are repaid, why should I as auditor treat this as debt rather than equity?
hostile.a: Because the obligation to repay is fixed and enforceable, only deferred. The agreement sets a maturity and a rate, the interest accrues whether or not it is paid, both companies record it as a liability and a receivable, and the subordination terms are the same ones unrelated mezzanine lenders accept. Here is the full evidence file. If after reading it you reach a different view, I would like our tax adviser to meet you before the accounts are signed.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 60 Review: Financing the Structure
summary: Six questions on shares versus loans, interest limits and sizing, a recap of the week, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a defective intercompany loan, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: decide whether your money goes in as shares or as a loan before it moves, prove it with documents made at the time, and size any loan to the tightest rule and the bank's terms.

Recall

Q. In the room, what is the question behind the bank counsel's subordination demands?

A. If this project goes wrong, can the sponsor's loan compete with ours for the building?

Q. What is a permanent establishment?

A. A fixed place of business or a dependent agent through which a foreign company carries on business in a country, giving that country the right under a treaty to tax the profits attributable to it.

Q. What is buyout in procurement?

A. The stage at which a contractor converts the budget into signed subcontracts and purchase orders, turning estimated costs into committed ones.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, financing the structure is where tax, banking and governance meet in one document. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can sit with your tax adviser, your auditor and your lender and follow every word. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name four reasons a parent might fund a project company with a shareholder loan rather than only shares.

Answer: Interest may be deductible where the project is; repayment of principal is usually not taxed as income; a loan can rank ahead of shares in insolvency; and a schedule disciplines how cash comes back.

Question 2. Why does the tax saving from a shareholder loan usually shrink on the way to the parent?

Answer: Because withholding tax may apply when the interest crosses the border, and the parent's country usually taxes the interest as income, perhaps with a credit for the withholding. Model it end to end.

Question 3. What are the four families of interest-limitation rules?

Answer: Ratio tests, earnings tests, arm's-length tests and recharacterisation. Each country writes them differently; verify against the primary source.

Question 4. Name five facts that make an intercompany advance look like real debt.

Answer: A written agreement made at the time; a fixed maturity and repayment schedule; interest actually paid or accrued as agreed; a borrower able to repay; terms an outside lender would accept; and consistent treatment in both companies' books and minutes.

Question 5. How do you size a shareholder loan?

Answer: Like a bank loan: compute the maximum under the ratio test, the earnings test and the bank's distribution test, check the rate is arm's length, and take the smallest result.

Question 6. What does the senior lender require of a shareholder loan, and why?

Answer: Subordination, a standstill, no payments during default and payments only when the distribution test is met, so that your loan can never compete with the bank's for the building.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Omar framed shares and loans as one design choice with consequences for tax, priority, banking and exit. Ford and Cole took apart a composite in which an undocumented advance was labelled a loan at tax time and backed by a backdated agreement, giving Rule 60. Nadia followed one year of cash home and showed the saving halving, and showed the principal at refinancing. Elias mapped the four families of interest-limitation rules and the facts that make debt real. Nadia reverse engineered the largest loan that survives every limit. Omar ran the meeting with the bank's counsel and the auditor.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 60 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical intercompany loan summary as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Intercompany Loan, Holdco to ProjectCo. Principal: up to 8,000,000 dollars, advanced as required. Interest: 9 percent, or such other rate as the parties may agree from time to time, payable when cash permits. Maturity: on demand. Security: none. Approved by: the director of Holdco. Effective date: 1 January, being the date of the first advance; agreement signed 30 June. Share capital of ProjectCo: 100 dollars.

The defects. First, "up to 8,000,000 dollars, advanced as required" leaves the amount undefined, so the auditor cannot test it against any ratio. Second, a rate the parties may change "from time to time" is not a fixed commercial term, and 9 percent has no supporting evidence attached. Third, "payable when cash permits" makes interest depend on profit, a classic feature of equity. Fourth, "on demand" with no schedule, combined with no security, shows no real expectation of repayment, and an on-demand loan will also conflict with the bank's standstill. Fifth, only Holdco's director approved it; there is no approval by ProjectCo as borrower. Sixth, it was signed in June but made effective from January; that may be acceptable as a written confirmation of an earlier arrangement, but only if it says so plainly, and the auditor will ask for evidence of the January terms. Seventh, 100 dollars of share capital against 8,000,000 dollars of debt is about as thin as capitalisation gets.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence behind each line: the bank records of every advance; the rate analysis; ProjectCo's board minutes; the cash-flow projection showing ability to repay; and the tax adviser's note on interest limits. A loan that cannot produce these is, in the auditor's file, equity with a story attached.

Cole adds one habit. When you review your own intercompany documents, read them twice: once as the author, checking that they say what you meant, and once as the stranger who will read them in three years with no memory of the conversation and every reason to doubt you. The second reading finds what the first one misses, because the author fills gaps from memory that the stranger can only fill from the page.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new partner who asks, "Why don't we just lend all our money into the project company and save the tax?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because the saving is smaller than it looks and the rules push back. Interest may be deductible where the project is, but withholding and tax at our end take back part of it. Most countries cap related-party interest, by a debt-to-equity ratio, by a share of earnings, or both, and during construction, when there are no earnings, an earnings cap can allow nothing. If we lend without documents, an authority can treat the whole thing as shares. And the bank will subordinate our loan and block payments whenever its test fails. So we decide the mix up front, size the loan to the tightest limit, document it with a dated agreement and both boards' approval, and model the cash all the way home, including the year the bank blocks us."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is deciding the form of your money after it has moved. The control is Rule 60, built into the bank mandate of your holding company.

The beginner's mistake

Treating "loan" and "shares" as labels you can swap later. They are legal facts, fixed by what you did at the time.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught minute books, resolutions and signing authority. The Auditor's Chair turned on exactly those: one company's director signed, the borrower never approved, and the date did not match the signature. Dull governance is what makes a loan a loan.

Recap

Shares and loans are one design choice. Loans can save tax but are capped, taxed on arrival and subordinated. Debt is real when it behaves like debt. Size to the binding limit, document before funding, and never backdate.

head: The six questions
speak: Financing the structure means deciding whether my money goes into the project company as shares or as a loan, before it moves. A loan can save tax where the project is, rank ahead of shares and give a repayment schedule. But the saving shrinks on the way home through withholding and tax at the parent's end, and most countries cap related-party interest with a ratio test, an earnings test or an arm's-length test, or treat the loan as shares if it does not behave like debt. Debt behaves like debt when there is a dated agreement, a maturity, interest paid or accrued as agreed, a borrower able to repay and consistent books. The bank will subordinate my loan and block payments when its test fails. So I size the loan to the tightest limit, document it with both boards' approval, model cash all the way home, and never backdate a document.
terms: Capitalisation — the mix of share capital and debt used to fund a company.
Interest limitation — tax rules that cap how much interest a company may deduct.
Intercompany loan — a loan between companies under common ownership, which must be documented and priced as if between strangers.
